prime.problem: This lecture is two hours of fixes to one small MLP, each with its own number and plot. Without a map it is easy to finish able to repeat the fixes but unable to say what they share: every one of them is about keeping activations and gradients at a sane scale, and knowing how to check that.
prime.fits: This card spans the whole course. It compresses the eleven cards into six claims. It builds on the z2h-4 MLP (the network being repaired), on micrograd's tanh backward (1 - t**2) * out.grad, and on the toolkit's mean and variance.
expect: the expected loss at step 0, ln 27 = 3.2958
tanh saturation and the 1 − t² gate
BatchNorm, its γ and β, and its running buffers
per-layer activation, gradient and update:data plots
prime.goal: Draw the lecture's repair log from memory, from the 27.88 step-0 loss to a BatchNorm deep stack with its three probes, and say for each symptom which fix or plot applies and what number it gave.

attend: Why does a random output layer make the step-0 loss 27.88 instead of 3.2958, and why does the loss eventually recover anyway?
The step-0 loss after fix 1 is 3.3221, yet 61% of the tanh units are saturated. What does the loss check miss, and which plot catches it?
Where does the √fan_in in Kaiming init come from, and what job is left for the gain 5/3?
If BatchNorm standardises every preactivation, why does it still need a learned γ and β, and why does a bias before it get zero gradient?
What forces BatchNorm to keep buffers that no gradient ever touches, and when do they get used?
BatchNorm makes the activation histograms look the same at any gain. Why does the update:data ratio still move?

must: The loss is −ln p(correct) → a net that knows nothing should give every character 1/27 → the step-0 target is ln 27 = 3.2958 → std-1 output weights make logits with std 12.75 that bet confidently on wrong characters (27.88) → W2 × 0.01, b2 × 0 gives 3.3221 and removes the hockey stick (val 2.1698 → 2.1311)

tanh backward multiplies by 1 − t² → near ±1 almost nothing gets through (0.0099 at t = 0.995) → with std-1 W1, hpreact has std about 5 and 61% of units saturate → shrink W1 so hpreact is about unit-sized → 1% saturated, val 2.1027; a unit saturated on every example is dead

A unit sums fan_in products → Var(y) = fan_in · Var(w) · Var(x) → std(w) = 1/√fan_in keeps the spread, and a gain undoes what the nonlinearity squeezes (5/3 for tanh) → W1 = (5/3)/√30 = 0.3043 with nothing tuned (val 2.1070) → but this only fixes step 0

Standardise each preactivation column with its batch mean and std, then γ·x̂ + β → unit-scale inputs to every nonlinearity on every step, whatever the weights → but each example now depends on its batchmates → test time needs fixed statistics: running buffers (EMA, momentum 0.001) that match calibration (val 2.1057 vs 2.1056)
elevated: BN divides out a Linear layer's weight scale → loss unchanged when W → c·W, so the gradient shrinks by c while std(W) grows by c → update:data moves by −2·log10 c (gain 0.2: +1.40) → the activation plots look healthy while the step size is 25× off, so the update:data plot is the one that shows it
reference: the loss log: val 2.1682 → 2.13 → 2.1027 → 2.1070 → 2.1048 (the lab reproduces 2.1057 for BN)
the 6-layer stack: 17 layer objects, 47,024 parameters (46,497 without BN)
the saturation thresholds: |h| > 0.99 in the imshow check, |t| > 0.97 in the histogram loop

compress.prompt: Card closed, one sheet of paper: draw the course's engine as the repair log of one MLP. Start from the starter net's step-0 loss, then add each fix in lecture order (output layer, tanh saturation, Kaiming init, BatchNorm with its buffers), and finish with the deep stack and the three probes you would attach to it. Beside each fix, write the symptom it cures and the number it gave.
checklist: step-0 target ln 27 = 3.2958 vs 27.88; the output-layer fix gives 3.3221
the tanh gate 1 − t², 61% → 1% saturated, and what a dead column means
std(w) = gain / √fan_in, tanh gain 5/3, W1 scale 0.3043
BatchNorm: batch mean and std, γ·x̂ + β, no bias before it, EMA buffers for test time
the probes: activation std and saturation per layer, gradient std per layer, update:data near −3 on log10
one line on why BatchNorm didn't beat Kaiming here (one hidden layer) but matters in deep stacks

retrieve.q: Explain why every fix in this lecture is really the same fix, and name the one thing BatchNorm does that the init fixes can't.
answer: each fix keeps a signal at a sane scale: logits near 0, preactivations about unit-sized, weights at gain/√fan_in
the init fixes set the scale at step 0 only; training can move the weights away
BatchNorm re-standardises on every forward pass, whatever the weights have become

retrieve.q: Walk one minibatch through a BatchNorm layer in training mode, then say what changes in eval mode.
answer: hpreact (32 × 200) = embcat @ W1, no bias
per column: subtract the batch mean, divide by the batch std
multiply by γ and add β (start at 1 and 0, trained by backprop)
under no_grad, nudge the running mean and std 0.1% toward this batch's
eval mode: use the running buffers instead of batch stats, so one example gives a fixed answer and no nan

retrieve.q: Your deep tanh net trains slowly. The step-0 loss is 3.30 and the activation histograms look healthy. Which diagnostic do you check next, what reading would confirm a too-small learning rate, and how would you fix it?
answer: the step-0 loss and histograms only check scale in the forward pass
plot log10(std(lr·grad) / std(w)) per weight matrix over time
curves well below −3 (e.g. −4.5 to −4.8 at lr 0.001) mean each step barely moves the weights
raise lr; each 10× moves every curve up by exactly 1

retrieve.q: BatchNorm didn't beat Kaiming init on the one-hidden-layer MLP (val 2.1057 vs 2.1070). Give the case for it anyway, and the costs Karpathy warns about.
answer: in deep stacks no hand-set scale survives many layers; BN keeps every layer standardised
it makes the forward pass gain-proof (activation std about 0.65 at gain 1 or 5/3)
costs: examples in a batch are coupled, a batch of 1 gives nan, train/eval mode and momentum bugs
alternatives that avoid the coupling: LayerNorm and GroupNorm

compare.q: The z2h-4 learning-rate finder and this lecture's update:data plot both help pick a learning rate. What does each one actually measure, which design choice makes the update:data plot able to spot a single bad layer, and how does each mislead you?
answer: the lr finder sweeps lr over steps and watches the whole-net loss
update:data measures each weight matrix's step relative to its own size, per step
because it is per tensor, one outlier (like a shrunk last layer) shows up; the loss can't show that
the finder is confounded by training progress during the sweep; −3 is a rule of thumb, not a law (Adam changes its meaning)

compare.q: micrograd's neuron has a tanh whose backward is (1 - t**2) * out.grad. What did that single line hide that this lecture had to deal with, and why didn't it matter for micrograd's tiny net?
answer: the factor 1 − t² can be close to 0, so a saturated unit passes almost no gradient
at 200 units with std-1 weights, hpreact has std about 5 and 61% of units saturate
micrograd's MLP(3, [4, 4, 1]) had few inputs per unit, so preactivations stayed small
at scale you have to control the preactivations' spread: init scaling, then BatchNorm

compare.q: The bigram lecture defined the loss as the average negative log likelihood. How does that same definition give you a free sanity check before training, and what does the check fail to catch?
answer: with no knowledge the model should give 1/V to every class, so the loss should be ln V (ln 27 = 3.2958)
a much larger step-0 loss means over-confident random logits, fixable at init
it says nothing about hidden layers: after fix 1 the loss was 3.3221 with 61% of tanh units saturated

predict.q: You stack 50 layers of Linear(100, 100) → tanh with no BatchNorm, weights randn / √100 times a gain. Commit first: at gain 1, is the tanh output std at layer 50 about 0.6, about 0.1, or about 0? And at gain 5/3?
predict.answer: At gain 1 it fades: std 0.635 at layer 1, 0.318 at layer 5, 0.153 at layer 20, 0.096 at layer 50, because every tanh squeezes and nothing undoes it. At gain 5/3 it holds: 0.764, then 0.650 from layer 5 on, 0.655 at layer 50. (Computed in scratch, one seeded batch of 32 unit-Gaussian inputs; not a lab number.) This is why the gain matters more the deeper you go, and why hand-balancing it was replaced by BatchNorm.

apply.task: Rebuild the lecture's loss log yourself. Start from your z2h-4 MLP (the starter net) and apply the fixes one at a time: W2 × 0.01 and b2 × 0; then W1 × 0.2 and b1 × 0.01; then replace the 0.2 with (5/3)/√30; then drop b1 and add BatchNorm with running buffers. After each change print the step-0 loss and the val loss after 200,000 steps, and write one line on which big idea the change uses.
apply.done: Your log reads step 0: 27.8817 → 3.3221 for the output fix, and val 2.1698 (starter) → 2.1311 → 2.1027 → 2.1070 → 2.1057 (BatchNorm, running stats), matching the labs on your M3 to about 0.001.
apply.hint: Keep the seed 2147483647 and the draw order C, W1, b1, W2, b2 so your numbers match. Each full run takes about 20–45 s on an idle M3; the labs with --quick check the step-0 numbers in seconds.

reflect: Which prediction did you get wrong: the 50-layer std at gain 1, or which way the update:data ratio moves under BatchNorm with gain 0.2?
Which panel could you not redraw from memory, and which number or arrow was missing?
Which relationship is still fuzzy: saturated tanh → vanishing gradient, or weight scale → saturation → the need for gain / √fan_in?
Could you explain to a friend why BatchNorm needs running buffers at test time, using the nan from a batch of one?
Which card will you reopen before the backprop-ninja lecture, where you will write BatchNorm's backward pass by hand?
